summary: Describes version 3 of the Network Time Protocol, its formal structure, and information useful for implementing it. NTP synchronizes computer clocks across the Internet. This version is historic and was replaced by RFC 5905.

plainLanguage.summary: NTP keeps clocks in step by measuring the difference between a local clock and a better one, and correcting the local clock. It runs over UDP, needs no connection, and recovers from losing packets by measuring again.

subtitle: Version 3 of the protocol that keeps computer clocks in step by measuring the difference between them and correcting the local clock.

tldr.problem: Clocks in different computers drift apart, and applications that care about time, ordering or security need a way to keep them aligned.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends a timestamped request to a time server and compares it with the timestamps in the reply, which yields the offset between the two clocks; a filter and a selection procedure then pick the best measurements and the best server.
tldr.outcome: The document specified the protocol, its algorithms and the analysis behind them, and became a Historic document. It was later obsoleted by RFC 5905.

facts.label: Modes of operation
facts.value: Symmetric active, symmetric passive, client, server, broadcast

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document is a formal specification of version 3 of the Network Time Protocol, which is used to synchronize timekeeping among a set of distributed time servers and clients. NTP was first described in RFC 958 and evolved through version 2 in RFC 1119. Version 3 neither changes the protocol in any significant way nor obsoletes previous versions or existing implementations. The main motivation for the new version is to refine the analysis and implementation models for applications at much higher network speeds and to provide the enhanced stability, accuracy and precision such speeds require. The sources of time and frequency errors have been examined and error bounds established, so that performance can be predicted, correctness assertions made, and timekeeping quality indicated to the user.

NTP is built on IP and UDP, which provide a connectionless transport mechanism, and it is readily adaptable to other protocol suites. It evolved from the Time Protocol and the ICMP Timestamp message, but is specifically designed to maintain accuracy and robustness even over typical Internet paths involving multiple gateways, highly dispersive delays and unreliable networks. The service model is a returnable-time design that depends only on measured clock offsets and does not require reliable message delivery. The synchronization subnet uses a self-organizing, hierarchical-master-slave configuration, with synchronization paths determined by a minimum-weight spanning tree. While multiple primary servers may exist, there is no requirement for an election protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: NTP keeps clocks in step by measuring the difference between a local clock and a better one, and correcting the local clock. It runs over UDP, needs no connection, and recovers from losing packets by measuring again.

sections.title: System Architecture
sections.content:
A number of primary reference sources, synchronized by wire or radio to national standards, are connected to widely accessible resources such as backbone gateways and operated as primary time servers. The purpose of NTP is to convey timekeeping information from these servers to other time servers over the Internet, and also to cross-check clocks and mitigate errors due to equipment or propagation failures. Some local-net hosts or gateways, acting as secondary time servers, run NTP with one or more of the primary servers, and to reduce protocol overhead the secondary servers distribute time to the remaining local-net hosts. Selected hosts can be equipped with less accurate but less expensive radio clocks and used as backup in case of failure of the primary or secondary servers or the paths between them.

The document uses a fixed vocabulary. The stability of a clock is how well it maintains a constant frequency; the accuracy is how well its frequency and time compare with national standards; and the precision is how precisely those quantities can be maintained within a particular timekeeping system. The offset of two clocks is the time difference between them, and the skew is the frequency difference between them.

NTP produces three products, all relative to a selected reference clock: clock offset, the amount to adjust the local clock to bring it into correspondence with the reference; roundtrip delay, which provides the capability to launch a message to arrive at the reference clock at a specified time; and dispersion, the maximum error of the local clock relative to the reference. Because most hosts synchronize through another peer, each of these has two components, the one determined by the peer relative to the primary reference and the one measured by the host relative to the peer, and each component is maintained separately in the protocol.

The accuracy of a server is defined by a number called the stratum, following a convention established in the telephone industry. The topmost level, the primary servers, is stratum one, and each level downwards in the hierarchy is assigned one greater than the preceding level. Under normal circumstances the synchronization subnet assumes a hierarchical-master-slave configuration with the primary servers at the root and secondary servers of decreasing accuracy at successive levels toward the leaves. There is no provision for peer discovery or virtual-circuit management; data integrity is provided by the IP and UDP checksums, and no flow-control or retransmission facilities are provided or necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: Time servers form a hierarchy. A server directly tied to a national standard is stratum one; each server that synchronizes to another server sits one level further from the standard. NTP measures the offset, the round-trip delay and the maximum error, and reports all three.

sections.title: Timestamps and the NTP Message Format
sections.content:
NTP timestamps are 64-bit unsigned fixed-point numbers in seconds relative to 0h on 1 January 1900, with the integer part in the first 32 bits and the fraction part in the last 32 bits. The precision of this representation is about 200 picoseconds. A timestamp is produced by copying the current value of the local clock when a significant event, such as the arrival of a message, occurs, and the copy is made as close to the hardware or software driver associated with the event as possible; departure timestamps should be redetermined for each link-level retransmission. Where a particular timestamp is not available, such as when the host is rebooted or the protocol first starts up, the 64-bit field is set to zero, indicating that the value is invalid or undefined. Since some time in 1968 the most significant bit of the integer part has been set, and the 64-bit field will overflow some time in 2036.

The NTP message data area, which immediately follows the UDP header, carries a two-bit leap indicator warning of an impending leap second, a three-bit version number currently three, a three-bit mode, an eight-bit stratum, an eight-bit poll interval giving the maximum interval between successive messages in seconds to the nearest power of two, an eight-bit precision, a 32-bit root delay giving the total roundtrip delay to the primary reference source, a 32-bit root dispersion giving the maximum error relative to the primary reference source, a 32-bit reference clock identifier, and four 64-bit timestamps: the reference timestamp, the local time at which the local clock was last set or corrected; the originate timestamp, the local time at which the request departed the client host; the receive timestamp, the local time at which the request arrived at the service host; and the transmit timestamp, the local time at which the reply departed the service host. An optional authenticator field follows when the authentication mechanism is implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: Each NTP message carries four timestamps: when the sender sent it, when the receiver got it, when the sender received the reply, and when it sent the reply. Comparing those gives the offset between the two clocks. The timestamp is a 64-bit number counting seconds since 1900, with 32 bits of fraction.

sections.title: Modes of Operation
sections.content:
Except in broadcast mode, an NTP association is formed when two peers exchange messages and one or both of them create and maintain an instantiation of the protocol machine. The association can operate in one of five modes, given by the host-mode variable. Symmetric active: the host sends periodic messages regardless of the reachability state or stratum of its peer, announcing its willingness to synchronize and to be synchronized by the peer. Symmetric passive: this association is ordinarily created on arrival of a message from a peer in symmetric active mode, and persists only as long as the peer is reachable and operating at a stratum less than or equal to the host, though it always persists until at least one message has been sent in reply. Client: the host sends periodic messages regardless of the reachability state or stratum of its peer, and announces its willingness to be synchronized by, but not to synchronize, the peer. Server: the association is ordinarily created on arrival of a client request message and exists only in order to reply to that request, after which it is dissolved. Broadcast: the host sends periodic messages regardless of the reachability state or stratum of the peers, and announces its willingness to synchronize all of them but not to be synchronized by any of them.

In the client/server modes the protocol machine can be simplified to a simple remote-procedure-call mechanism without significant loss of accuracy or robustness, especially when operating over high-speed LANs. Servers need retain no state information between client requests, while clients are free to manage the intervals between sending NTP messages to suit local conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: Two hosts that exchange NTP messages form an association, and the association can run in five ways. In the simplest, the client asks and the server answers and forgets; in the symmetric modes the two sides are nearly indistinguishable.

sections.title: Access Control and Authentication
sections.content:
The NTP design is such that accidental or malicious data modification, tampering, or destruction at a time server should not in general result in timekeeping errors elsewhere in the synchronization subnet. This depends on redundant time servers and diverse network paths, together with the assumption that tampering will not occur at many time servers throughout the subnet at the same time. In principle the subnet vulnerability can be engineered through the selection of time servers known to be trusted and allowing only those to become the synchronization source.

The optional authentication procedures are one mechanism for enforcing this. When it is created and possibly at other times, each association is allocated variables identifying the certificate authority, the encryption algorithm and the cryptographic key. The authenticator field consists of two subfields, a key identifier and a crypto-checksum, and its presence is revealed by the total datagram length according to the UDP header being longer than the NTP message length. The cryptographic keys are a set of 64-bit DES keys, and by convention the unspecified key of eight odd-parity zero octets is used for testing and is presumed known throughout the NTP community.

The document notes that the encryption algorithms can be quite CPU-intensive and can seriously degrade accuracy unless precautions are taken. Some implementations may also include an access-control feature that prevents unauthorized access and controls which peers are allowed to update the local clock, distinguishing accesses preauthorized as trusted, preauthorized as friendly and all other accesses. Only trusted accesses can result in the peer becoming the synchronization source.
sections.plainLanguage: NTP is built to survive a bad or dishonest time server, because other servers disagree and the disagreeing one gets thrown out. The optional authentication adds a keyed checksum to each message so a receiver can tell a genuine message from a forged one.

sections.title: Filtering and Selection Algorithms
sections.content:
The NTP algorithms have two stages: a clock-filter procedure that selects the best offset samples from a given clock, and a clock-selection procedure that selects the best clock among a hierarchical set of clocks. The clock filter is a shift register of NTP.SHIFT stages, each stage holding a triple of offset, delay and dispersion. New samples are shifted in at the left, causing first empty stages and then old samples to fall off the right, and the dispersion of every valid sample is updated to account for the skew-error accumulation since the last update. The samples are then sorted by increasing distance, and the procedure determines the filtered offset, delay and dispersion for that peer.

The clock-selection procedure consists of two algorithms. The intersection algorithm constructs a list of candidate peers eligible to become the synchronization source, computes a confidence interval for each, and casts out falsetickers using a technique adapted from Marzullo and Owicki. Each peer that passes the sanity checks contributes three endpoints to a list that is sorted by increasing endpoint, and the algorithm looks for the largest single intersection containing only truechimers; if fewer than half the candidates are truechimers, the procedure is repeated with a larger interval. The clustering algorithm then sorts the surviving candidates in order of stratum and synchronization distance and repeatedly casts out outliers on the basis of select dispersion until only the most accurate, precise and stable survivors are left. The system variable holding the peer is then set to point at the most likely survivor, or to the null value if there is none.
sections.plainLanguage: Each server keeps a short history of the offset measurements it has received from one peer, and discards the worst ones. Then it compares the servers it knows: it computes the range of times that most of them agree on, throws out the ones that disagree, and among those left picks the one closest to a national standard with the smallest error.

viz.caption: THE NTP MESSAGE FIELDS FROM RFC 1305, APPENDIX A

fields.name: Leap Indicator
fields.desc: 00 no warning, 01 the last minute has 61 seconds, 10 the last minute has 59 seconds, 11 an alarm condition meaning the clock is not synchronized.

fields.name: Version Number
fields.desc: The NTP version number, currently three (3).

fields.name: Mode
fields.desc: 0 reserved, 1 symmetric active, 2 symmetric passive, 3 client, 4 server, 5 broadcast, 6 reserved for an NTP control message, 7 reserved for private use.

fields.name: Stratum
fields.desc: 0 unspecified, 1 a primary reference such as a radio clock, 2 to 255 a secondary reference via NTP.

fields.name: Poll Interval
fields.desc: The maximum interval between successive messages, in seconds to the nearest power of two.

fields.name: Precision
fields.desc: The precision of the local clock, in seconds to the nearest power of two.

fields.name: Root Delay
fields.desc: The total roundtrip delay to the primary reference source.

fields.name: Root Dispersion
fields.desc: The maximum error relative to the primary reference source.

fields.name: Reference Clock Identifier
fields.desc: A code identifying the particular reference clock.

fields.name: Reference Timestamp
fields.desc: The local time at which the local clock was last set or corrected.

fields.name: Originate Timestamp
fields.desc: The local time at which the request departed the client host.

fields.name: Receive Timestamp
fields.desc: The local time at which the request arrived at the service host.

fields.name: Transmit Timestamp
fields.desc: The local time at which the reply departed the service host.

viz.caption: THE FIVE NTP ASSOCIATION MODES (RFC 1305, SECTION 3.3)

items.label: Symmetric active
items.desc: Sends periodic messages regardless of the peer's reachability or stratum; willing to synchronize and to be synchronized by the peer.

items.label: Symmetric passive
items.desc: Created on arrival of a message from a symmetric active peer; persists while that peer is reachable and at a stratum less than or equal to the host.

items.label: Client
items.desc: Sends periodic messages and announces its willingness to be synchronized by, but not to synchronize, the peer.

items.label: Server
items.desc: Created on arrival of a client request and exists only in order to reply to it.

items.label: Broadcast
items.desc: Sends periodic messages to all peers, willing to synchronize them but not to be synchronized by any of them.
